# References

# Evaluating the Preprocessing Methods {.appendix}

The Data Preprocessing section recommended the mixture method with an ex-Gaussian core distribution followed by the accuracy adjustment, the robust statistics as a deliberate alternative, and no hard pre-filtering before aggregation. This appendix reports the evidence for those recommendations, organized by the route a reader takes: first what the methods do to the summary statistics an `ezdm` analysis consumes, then what the exclusion rules do to the trial sets a `cswald` or `ddm` analysis consumes. The companion scripts are `scripts/02_simulation_contaminant_methods.R` for the Monte Carlo study, `scripts/02b_simulation_validation_ezdm.R` for its validation with hierarchical `ezdm()` fits, `scripts/10_tutorial0_data_preprocessing.R` for the contaminant-bias demonstration, and `scripts/10b_preprocessing_comparison.R` for the systematic comparison of flagging settings.

## What Contaminants Do to the Summary Statistics

The three contaminant processes are best seen before they are scored. @fig-rt-density shows where each one places its trials in a single simulated dataset (50 participants, 200 trials per condition, drift 2.5 in the easy and 1.0 in the hard condition, bound 1.5, ndt 0.3 s, 3% of trials replaced per process). Leading-edge anticipations straddle the fast end of the core distribution rather than sitting below it: in this dataset only 3.5% of them fall below a 180 ms cutoff and 29% below 250 ms, so neither a hard cutoff nor a mixture model gets a free case. Delayed start-ups spread across and beyond the slow tail; informationless responses sit almost on top of the core distribution, particularly in the hard condition.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rt-density
#| fig-cap: "Where the three contaminant processes place their trials, relative to the RT distribution the decision process produces. Each panel shows the core distribution (grey) and the injected contaminants (orange); both are scaled to the same area, so the panels compare the location of the two components rather than their relative frequency (contaminants are 3% of trials per process). Leading-edge anticipations straddle the fast edge of the core, delayed start-ups partly overlap it, and informationless responses overlap it almost completely."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "10_rt_density.pdf"))
```

@fig-sumstats-bias shows the downstream consequence: contaminated data produce inflated RT variance, shifted mean RT, and reduced accuracy. Because EZ-Diffusion parameters are direct transformations of these summary statistics, any distortion propagates straight into biased parameter estimates. The rest of this appendix quantifies that propagation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sumstats-bias
#| fig-cap: "Comparison of summary statistics (mean RT, variance of RT, accuracy) computed from contaminated versus clean data. Each box spans the interquartile range across 50 simulated participants. Contaminant responses inflate RT variance, shift mean RT, and reduce accuracy."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "10_sumstats_bias.pdf"))
```

## Comparing Preprocessing Methods

The Monte Carlo study, run with `SimDesign` [@chalmers2020simdesign] and structured after the ADEMP framework (aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods, performance measures; @morris2019simulation), simulated 50 participants who completed 50 or 200 trials in an easy and a hard condition (population drift 2.5 and 1.0; bound 1.5 and ndt 0.3 s, the same in both conditions; participant-level random effects on all three). Contaminants replaced a share of each participant's trials, drawn from three processes that differ in their psychological source and in how far they overlap the core RT distribution.

*Leading-edge anticipations* represent premature responding. Each participant draws an anticipation depth $x_i \sim U(0.1, 0.5)$, shared across conditions, and each contaminated trial receives an RT uniform on $((1 - x_i)\tau_i, (1 + x_i)\tau_i)$ with the response at chance — a band centred on that participant's own non-decision time [adapted from @lerche2017trials]. This construct deliberately denies both tools under test an easy case: the contaminants straddle the hard cutoffs and the core's leading edge rather than forming a separable spike beneath them. *Delayed start-ups* add a delay uniform on 0 to 2 s to a genuine decision RT and keep the response, the convention since @ratcliff2002estimating that also underlies the original validation of robust-EZ [@wagenmakers2008extensions]. *Informationless responses* redraw the trial from a diffusion process with zero drift [@vandekerckhove2008bayesian; @chavez2026robust], so their RTs overlap the core completely and their accuracy is at chance.

The three pure processes were run at 2% and 10% contamination as mechanism diagnostics. The primary condition is a fourth, *mixed* one, which drops the assumption that every participant is contaminated in the same way and at the same rate: each participant draws a total contamination rate from a Beta distribution (concentration 10, so at a mean of 5% the rates spread over roughly 0–25% — many near-clean participants and a minority of heavy contaminators) and a mix over the three processes from a uniform Dirichlet distribution, both held constant across that participant's two conditions. This is the only condition in which contamination varies *between* participants, and therefore the only one that genuinely stresses the individual-difference estimands. It was run at mean rates of 2%, 5%, and 10%, and a clean baseline is shared across all processes. The design comprises 20 rows of 200 replications each, with common random numbers so that differences between rows reflect the contaminants rather than sampling.

The estimand — the quantity each method is scored against — was not the summary statistics themselves, because the clean sample moments are a target the plain moments (`simple`) hit by construction and the median cannot, but the generating drift, bound, and ndt of every participant × condition cell, obtained by passing each method's statistics through the closed-form EZ equations [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion], the same equations `ezdm()` uses, together with two practical estimands: the easy − hard drift difference and the correlation between participant-level estimates and their generating values. Bias and RMSE were computed over 200 replications, and an oracle that computes the plain moments after perfect contaminant exclusion marks the best any flagging method could achieve. Throughout this appendix a difference is called substantial only if it exceeds twice the Monte Carlo standard error of the study.

On clean data the mixture method recovers all three parameters with negligible bias, whereas the median and IQR-based statistics carry a two-sided offset: in the easy condition they inflate drift by +0.26 and deflate bound by −0.14, leaving ndt essentially intact, so that the drift contrast is inflated (+0.13 on a true difference of about 1.5). The reason the offset lands where it does is that RT distributions are right-skewed, so the median falls below the mean and the IQR-based variance below the variance; when the EZ equations turn these statistics into parameters, the smaller variance shortens the implied decision time by about as much as the median falls short of the mean, which leaves ndt almost unchanged and pushes the whole discrepancy into drift and bound. That the offset is two-sided matters for reading the results below: because contamination attenuates drift, the drift half of the offset can mask attenuation at some contamination rates while the bound half compounds. The lognormal and inverse-Gaussian cores are misspecified for diffusion RTs: even without contamination they flag about 2% of trials as contaminants and return drift and bound biases as large as the robust method's (+0.28 and −0.14), with a further ndt bias the robust statistics do not have. That is why the ex-Gaussian is the default core.

```{r}
#| label: fig-simulation-methods
#| fig-cap: "Signed bias in the EZ-Diffusion parameters recovered by each preprocessing method (estimate − generating value; 200 replications, 200 trials per cell) by contaminant process (columns), parameter (rows), and contamination rate. Solid lines: easy condition; dashed lines: hard condition. The oracle computes the plain moments after perfect contaminant exclusion. Points are means over participants and replications; Monte Carlo standard errors are at most 0.03."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "02_method_comparison.pdf"))
```

@fig-simulation-methods shows the bias in the three parameters for each pure process. Three patterns organize the results, and all values quoted here are easy-condition values at 10% contamination with 200 trials per cell unless stated otherwise.

First, whether a method helps depends entirely on whether the contaminants can be detected, and detection depends on where they sit. Delayed start-ups are the favourable case: the plain moments break down (drift −0.80, bound +0.68, ndt −0.21) while the mixture method recovers a contaminant proportion close to the truth (5.3% of a true 10%) and cuts the drift bias to −0.22, the accuracy adjustment takes it to −0.02, and the robust statistics stay within their offset (−0.04). Leading-edge anticipations are the unfavourable case: the mixture recovers almost none of the proportion (0.4%), because a core distribution wide enough to cover them is also a defensible fit, and every method that depends on detection therefore lands where the plain moments do (−0.47 for the mixture, −0.46 with the adjustment, against −0.50 uncorrected). Informationless responses sit in between only because they are frequent enough to shift the moments detectably (proportion 0.7%, drift −0.58 for the mixture against −0.69 uncorrected).

Second, contaminants reach the EZ equations through two channels, the RT distribution and the proportion correct, and down-weighting reaches only the first. A trial answered at chance lowers the proportion correct whatever happens to its RT, and at the accuracy level of an easy condition this channel dominates. This is what `adjust_ezdm_accuracy()` addresses, and its pattern across processes follows the reach of detection rather than the correctness of its assumption. It helps most under delayed start-ups (drift −0.22 → −0.02) even though its chance-accuracy assumption is *wrong* there — flagged delays carry genuine decisions — because reclassifying them still removes more of the accuracy distortion than it adds; at 10% it overshoots the contrast into positive bias (+0.06) while reducing its magnitude relative to the mixture (−0.11). Under informationless responses, where the assumption is exactly right, it moves little (−0.58 → −0.55), because the flags are almost never raised. This is the opposite of what we predicted before running the study, and the reason is worth stating: the adjustment's reach is set by detection, not by whether its model of the contaminant is correct.

Third, participant-level correlations are far less affected than mean levels. Under every pure process at 10%, drift correlations stay at .87 or above for the mixture, adjusted mixture, and robust methods, while the plain moments fall to .69 under informationless responses. This is the practical estimand, and it degrades much more slowly than absolute bias — which is why the recommendations rest on it.

Hard cutoffs act on exactly one thing: the contaminants that lie beyond them, and the leading-edge process is designed so that few do. The conventional cutoffs of the original @wagenmakers2008lexical analysis (RT < 180 ms or > 3 s) barely move any process — under 10% anticipations they take the plain moments' drift bias from −0.50 to −0.48, under delays from −0.80 to −0.79, under informationless responses from −0.69 to −0.66. The aggressive variant (250 ms / 2.5 s) does better on anticipations (−0.37), because a larger share of that band falls below 250 ms, and it is the least-biased pipeline in that one cell. That is not a reason to adopt it. Its gain is bought at the price @ulrich1994effects predicted, and the price is visible on wholly *clean* data, where the upper cutoff truncates the slow tail of the hard condition's legitimate RTs: bound −0.07 and ndt +0.03, against −0.04 and +0.02 for the conventional cutoffs and essentially zero without them. A method that wins in the one regime where the alternatives fail, and damages clean data, fails the criterion set out in the main text: it is not a defensible default when the analyst cannot know which regime they are in. Nor do cutoffs improve what follows them: running them before the mixture method or before flagging changed the drift contrast by at most 0.012 in any cell, well inside the Monte Carlo error of the study.

With 50 trials per cell the ordering of the methods is unchanged and every estimate is noisier (drift correlations .58–.89, ndt correlations .32–.55 in the mixed condition at 5%). One implementation detail matters throughout: the mixture EM was run with `maxit = 500` (the next subsection reports why), and in about one cell in 10^5^ the ex-Gaussian fit ran away to an implausible solution, which the study screened out by requiring the fitted mean to lie within the observed RT range.

## How Many EM Iterations, and Which Core Distribution

Because bmm's EM is deterministic and `maxit` is only the iteration cap, a single fit run to 500 iterations records what any lower cap would have produced: a cell converges under a cap of $k$ exactly if it converged within $k$ iterations, and otherwise receives the robust-moment fallback. The study therefore reports convergence at all three caps, and the parameter estimates each cap would have yielded, from one pass.

At bmm's default cap of 100 the EM fails to converge in 3.7% to 13.9% of cells with an ex-Gaussian core, depending on the process, rate, condition, and trial count; the inverse-Gaussian and lognormal cores span a similar range (2.0–16.5% and 2.0–18.3%). Raising the cap to 250 brings the worst cell to 2.6% for the ex-Gaussian core and 3.5% for the other two, and a cap of 500 brings all three to at most 0.5%. The three cores are, in other words, comparably reliable numerically, and the ex-Gaussian is marginally the best rather than the worst of them.

Non-convergence is not a fixed property of the method but a function of the data. With an ex-Gaussian core the failure rate at a cap of 100 runs from 3.7% (easy condition, 200 trials) to 7.5% (hard condition, 50 trials) on clean data, and reaches 13.9% under 10% delayed start-ups. The cap therefore bites hardest where preprocessing is most needed, and because `ezdm_summary_stats()` answers a failed fit by silently substituting robust moments, roughly one cell in seven in such a dataset would be aggregated by a method the analyst did not choose — and, in the trial-level pipeline, dropped entirely by a filter on `NA` probabilities. This is what `maxit = 500` is for.

What the alternative cores do buy is speed. One ex-Gaussian fit costs 33–114 ms against 5–22 ms for a lognormal and 10–32 ms for an inverse-Gaussian fit, a factor of roughly 3–6. The difference is not in the number of iterations — all three average between 21 and 70 — but in the cost of each density evaluation. Against the hours a hierarchical fit takes, none of this is material, so the choice of core should rest on bias, where the ex-Gaussian is the only one of the three that is unbiased on clean data.

## Which Trials the Flags Actually Catch

Scoring `flag_contaminant_rts()` against the known contaminant labels separates two error rates that the estimated contaminant proportion runs together. Specificity is uniformly high: across every process, rate, condition, and trial count it is at least .993, so flags are rare among trials that are not contaminants. Sensitivity is low and highly variable. In the easy condition with 200 trials it is .34–.40 for delayed start-ups and .05 or below for informationless responses, the latter being the case no RT-based rule can reach. For leading-edge anticipations it is .16 at a 2% rate and .008 at 10%: as anticipations become more frequent, the fitted core distribution stretches far enough to cover them and they stop being flagged at all. Detection is therefore worst where contamination is heaviest, which is the opposite of what one would want. All of these are easy-condition values; the hard condition is worse throughout, because a slower, broader core absorbs more.

Precision spans nearly the whole range, from .05 to .97, and is routinely below .5 in the hard condition — under 10% anticipations it is .24 in the easy condition and .05 in the hard one. No single figure therefore summarizes how trustworthy an individual flag is, and this is why the recommendation in the main text rests on specificity instead: what licenses discarding a flagged trial is not that the flag is probably right, but that at this specificity the procedure discards at most about 0.7% of legitimate trials even when it is wrong. Monte Carlo standard errors on all of these are at most .018.

## The Trial-Level Route: Which Trials Survive

A `cswald` or `ddm` analysis does not consume summary statistics; it consumes a set of trials. The question for that reader is therefore not which aggregation method corrects which channel, but what is left in the data after an exclusion rule has run — and the answer has to be given in terms the likelihood can see. Three measures do that: whether the two exclusion rules leave the same set behind, how the surviving trials deviate from the same cell's uncontaminated trials, and where the surviving contaminants sit.

**The two rules are interchangeable in their consequences, not in the trials they remove.** They agree on 97.3% to 99.95% of individual keep/drop decisions, yet the sets they exclude overlap only partially: the Jaccard overlap of the excluded sets runs from .34 to .60, and is already around .36 in the clean rows, so the disagreement is a property of how the rules treat borderline probabilities rather than a consequence of contamination. Exclusions the model is confident about coincide; borderline ones do not. For a trial-level model this matters only through the surviving set as a distribution, because the DDM and Censored-Shifted Wald likelihoods treat trials within a cell as exchangeable — the fit depends on which trials survive only through their joint distribution, not on their identity. At that level the two rules are equivalent: their surviving sets deviate from the uncontaminated benchmark by nearly identical amounts (mean absolute eCDF deviation within .002 of each other in every cell, against pipeline-level deviations that reach .054), retain true contaminants at rates within .001 of each other, and match within .0005 in the sub-ndt region defined below. The largest difference that exceeds twice the Monte Carlo error — a drift bias of −0.17 versus −0.19 under 10% delayed start-ups, slightly favouring the threshold rule, on which the eCDF measure disagrees in direction — is an order of magnitude smaller than the difference either rule makes against no preprocessing at all (−0.49). @fig-ecdf-calibration shows the location-resolved deviations.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ecdf-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Distributional calibration of the trials each exclusion pipeline leaves behind, under mixed contamination with 200 trials per cell. Each panel plots the deviation of the surviving trials' empirical CDF from that of the same cell's uncontaminated trials, read at the uncontaminated quantiles; zero is perfect calibration and positive values indicate surplus mass below that location. Rows show the mean contamination rate, columns the condition. Ribbons are ±2 Monte Carlo standard errors."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "02_ecdf_calibration.pdf"))
```

**What survives matters more for trial-level models than for aggregation, and for a specific reason.** Among the trials a pipeline keeps, some are still contaminants — under 10% anticipations, about 10% of surviving trials are, and roughly half of those fall *below* the participant's true non-decision time. A slow contaminant merely leans on the tail of the likelihood, where the density is small but positive. A surviving trial faster than ndt is different in kind, and the three models handle it differently. In the full DDM both response branches evaluate `wiener_lpdf`, which requires the RT to exceed ndt, so such a trial has zero likelihood regardless of which response it carries; the same holds for the competing-risks Censored-Shifted Wald, where every branch contributes a shifted-Wald density term. In both cases the trial does not bias the estimate so much as *force* it: ndt is pushed below the fastest surviving RT, and bound and drift absorb the consequences. Under the simple Censored-Shifted Wald the contribution is response-dependent: a correct response hits the same catastrophe, while an error response contributes the log survival function, which at an RT below ndt equals zero — the largest value a log survival can take — so that trial instead exerts *upward* pressure on ndt. Because anticipation responses are generated at chance independently of their RT, half of the sub-ndt survivors fall in each case, and the two halves push in opposite directions. This is what the likelihoods imply, verified against `bmm`'s Stan source; whether the upward pressure is large enough to matter in a fitted hierarchical model was not simulated here.

**A lower cutoff is therefore worth applying before trial-level fitting, even though it does nothing for aggregation.** It is the only step in the study that reduces the sub-ndt zone at all: under 10% anticipations the aggressive lower cutoff roughly halves it (2.7% of surviving trials against 4.9% for flagging alone), and it does so on every process, because trials below ndt are by construction fast enough for a lower cutoff to reach. Flagging adds essentially nothing on top of a cutoff here (4.5% with flags against 4.5% without). This is a narrow recommendation and it does not rehabilitate cutoffs generally: the upper cutoff still carries the truncation cost documented above and is not recommended, and the lower cutoff is worth applying not because it improves parameter recovery — it does not, measurably — but because it removes trials the likelihood cannot represent at all.

**The flagging step cannot substitute for either.** Sensitivity to leading-edge anticipations is .12 when they make up 2% of trials and .004 at 10%, so both exclusion rules pass the sub-ndt zone through nearly untouched: 4.9% of surviving trials at a 10% rate, against the roughly 5% that would survive with no flagging at all — a figure that follows analytically from the generating band, since half of each participant's anticipations fall below their ndt by construction. The exclusion rules fail precisely on the trials that hurt the trial-level likelihood most. Protection has to come from the design and from the lower cutoff, not from the flags.

If you cannot rule out anticipations in your design, one cheap check is available before committing to an expensive fit: compute the closed-form EZ estimates under two different lower cutoffs and report whether ndt moves between them. A material shift indicates that the leading edge carries mass the decision process cannot produce, which the trial-level fit will inherit. This is a comparison to report, not a decision rule with a threshold — we did not study its error rates as a diagnostic, and it should not be treated as a test.

## Preprocessing Under Realistic Mixed Contamination

The pure-process conditions ask how well each method handles one contaminant mechanism at a time, with every participant contaminated equally. Real data do neither: one participant mostly anticipates, another mostly lapses, a third is nearly clean. The mixed condition implements this — each participant draws a total rate (Beta, spread roughly 0–25% at a mean of 5%) and a mix over the three processes (uniform Dirichlet) — and turns the comparison around to face the choice a user actually has: no preprocessing, hard cutoffs alone, `bmm`'s model-based tools alone, or cutoffs followed by a model-based step. This is the study's primary condition, and the recommendations rest on it. @fig-mixed-pipelines shows the parameter biases across the three mean rates, and @tbl-simulation-practical the practical estimands at the central rate.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mixed-pipelines
#| fig-cap: "Signed bias in the EZ-Diffusion parameters under mixed contamination, where each participant draws their own contamination rate and their own mix of the three processes. Rows show the mean contamination rate (2%, 5%, 10%), columns the parameter; points are means over 200 replications, coloured by condition and shaped by trial count. Cutoffs-only pipelines barely move the estimates; the model-based pipelines come closest to the oracle."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "02_mixed_pipelines.pdf"))
```

Three results order the pipelines; values are easy-condition, 200 trials per cell, at the 5% mean rate unless stated otherwise. First, cutoffs alone are not preprocessing: on drift they recover almost nothing (−0.35 for the conventional and −0.31 for the aggressive cutoffs, against −0.36 with no preprocessing and −0.15 to −0.22 for the model-based pipelines). Within the cocktail the flags reach the same components as in the pure conditions — sensitivity .38 for delayed start-ups, .09 for anticipations, .06 for informationless responses, with precision .90 — so what the mixture model could and could not see transfers cleanly to the realistic case.

Second, the accuracy-adjusted mixture is the best real method on the estimands that matter. It puts drift at −0.15 and the drift contrast at −0.10, against −0.22 and −0.16 for the mixture alone, −0.19 and −0.13 for flag-and-exclude, and −0.36 and −0.28 with no preprocessing; the oracle sits at +0.02 and 0.00. It also has the highest subject-level drift correlation of any real pipeline (.83, against .82 for the mixture, .81 for exclusion, .80 for the robust statistics, and .65 uncorrected). Adding cutoffs before any of these changes nothing beyond Monte Carlo error. The robust statistics land nearest zero on the contrast (−0.03) at this particular intensity, but that is the cancellation described above rather than a repair: their drift bias is +0.02 because a +0.26 offset is meeting an attenuation of similar size, and their bound bias (−0.19) does not benefit from the coincidence. At a 10% mean rate the same cancellation has moved on and the robust contrast bias is −0.18, against −0.19 for the adjusted mixture. With 50 trials per cell the ordering is unchanged, only noisier.

Third, and most sobering: preprocessing does not repair differential bias. Because contamination varies between participants here, each participant's drift error tracks their own contamination rate, and that correlation survives every pipeline. At the 5% mean rate it is −.74 in the easy condition with no preprocessing, and the best pipeline — the adjusted mixture — still leaves −.56, against .01 for the oracle; across all pipelines, rates, and conditions the residual correlation runs from −.32 to −.80. What preprocessing changes is the *composition* of that residual, not its presence. The partial correlation of drift error with a participant's count of zero-drift contaminants, holding their total count constant, is −.01 with no preprocessing but −.18 for the mixture, −.17 for threshold exclusion, and −.24 with the accuracy adjustment (twice the Monte Carlo error is about .03). Each pipeline repairs the share it can detect and thereby concentrates what remains in the share no RT-based rule can see; the accuracy adjustment shows the trade most clearly, weakening the overall correlation more than any other pipeline while showing the strongest concentration. These magnitudes are specific to this configuration — Beta-distributed participant rates, uniform process mix, 200 trials — and are weaker in the hard condition, where a broader RT distribution absorbs contaminants of every kind. The direction, however, is general: a participant who contaminates more is estimated worse under every pipeline we simulated. For individual-differences applications the protection has to come from the design side [@boag2025expert], not from the analysis.

Fitting `bmm`'s hierarchical `ezdm()` to one dataset per process — including the mixed process — reproduces the closed-form pattern rather than softening it. Posterior means differ from the closed-form estimates by at most 0.03 for drift and 0.005 s for ndt, and by about 0.06 for bound, where hierarchical shrinkage pulls in a badly inflated estimate; the ranking of the methods is unchanged, with the adjusted mixture again the best real method on the drift contrast (−0.09, against −0.13 for the mixture and −0.26 with no preprocessing). Partial pooling does not repair the differential bias either. It compresses the participant-level errors as expected — their standard deviation falls from 0.28 to 0.20 in the easy condition of the mixed dataset — but the correlation between a participant's drift error and their true contamination rate does not weaken with it, and for most methods slightly strengthens (for the mixture, −.71 closed-form against −.73 hierarchical in the easy condition). The explanation is that shrinkage removes idiosyncratic sampling noise, which is unrelated to how contaminated a participant is, leaving the systematic component a larger share of what remains. We had predicted this correlation would weaken; it did not, and we report the outcome against the prediction rather than the reverse. These are single-dataset illustrations against the Monte Carlo study's 200 replications, and should be read as such (`scripts/02b_simulation_validation_ezdm.R`).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-simulation-practical
#| tbl-cap: "Practical estimands under mixed contamination at a mean rate of 5% with 200 trials per cell (200 replications): bias and RMSE of the easy − hard drift difference (true difference ≈ 1.5), correlations between participant-level estimates and generating values (drift by condition; bound and ndt averaged over conditions), and the proportion of trials the mixture-based methods estimated as contaminants (true mean rate 5%). Pipelines are listed in the order of @fig-mixed-pipelines. Oracle: plain moments after perfect contaminant exclusion."
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
sim_sum <- readr::read_csv(here("data", "simulation_preprocessing_summary.csv"),
                           show_col_types = FALSE)

# The pipeline roster of @fig-mixed-pipelines, so table and figure cross-reference
# row for row. The mean rate of 5% exists only in the mixed condition of the v7
# design, which is why this table is mixed-only by construction.
tab_pipelines <- c(
  "Simple", "Simple, pre-filtered", "Simple, aggressive pre-filter",
  "Robust", "Mixture (ex-Gaussian)",
  "Mixture (ex-Gaussian) + accuracy adjustment",
  "Threshold exclusion (p > .5)", "Pre-filter + threshold exclusion",
  "Oracle (perfect exclusion)"
)
tab_labels <- c(
  "No preprocessing", "Conventional cutoffs", "Aggressive cutoffs",
  "Robust", "Mixture", "Mixture + accuracy adjustment",
  "Flag and exclude", "Cutoffs + flag and exclude", "Oracle"
)

sim_tab <- sim_sum |>
  dplyr::filter(p_contam == 0.05, n_trials == 200,
                stringr::str_starts(process, "Mixed"),
                method %in% tab_pipelines,
                measure %in% c("bias_effect", "rmse_effect", "cor_drift",
                               "cor_bound", "cor_ndt", "pi_c")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(key = dplyr::if_else(condition == "All", measure,
                                     paste(measure, condition, sep = "_"))) |>
  dplyr::select(method, key, value) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = key, values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::mutate(method = factor(method, levels = tab_pipelines,
                                labels = tab_labels)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(method)

# Guard: a silently changed design grid must break the render, not the table.
stopifnot(nrow(sim_tab) == length(tab_pipelines),
          !anyNA(sim_tab$method), !anyNA(sim_tab$bias_effect))

sim_tab <- sim_tab |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Pipeline = as.character(method),
    `Drift effect: bias (RMSE)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", bias_effect, rmse_effect),
    `r drift, easy` = sprintf("%.2f", cor_drift_Easy),
    `r drift, hard` = sprintf("%.2f", cor_drift_Hard),
    `r bound` = sprintf("%.2f", (cor_bound_Easy + cor_bound_Hard) / 2),
    `r ndt` = sprintf("%.2f", (cor_ndt_Easy + cor_ndt_Hard) / 2),
    Estimated = dplyr::if_else(is.na(pi_c_Easy), "",
                               sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (pi_c_Easy + pi_c_Hard) / 2))
  )
knitr::kable(sim_tab, align = "lcccccc")
```

@chavez2026robust ask a complementary question with the plain moments and the median/IQR statistics but without a mixture method, tracing contamination through to hypothesis tests on drift effects. The two studies agree where they overlap: the plain moments break down under contamination, contamination attenuates drift effects toward zero and thereby inflates Type II error rates, and the damage is worst when drift is high and RTs fast, so that easy tasks are the ones where preprocessing matters most — the opposite of the intuition that clean, high-accuracy data need less care. Their conclusion that the robust variant costs nothing on clean data holds for their estimand, tests on drift effects, and not for absolute parameter values, where on clean data it inflates drift and deflates bound by roughly a tenth in each direction. We read the two methods as trading precision in different places rather than as competitors: the robust statistics accept a known offset in exchange for not depending on detection, while the adjusted mixture is unbiased on clean data but limited by what the EM can see.

## Validation Against Published Exclusion Criteria

The simulation above establishes that the mixture method works under controlled conditions where the ground truth is known. Whether it also works on real data, where the true contamination rate is unknown, is a separate question. We can address it by validating the method against the exclusion criteria used in the original @wagenmakers2008lexical study, which removed trials with RT < 180 ms or RT > 3000 ms — a standard hard-cutoff approach.

Applying `flag_contaminant_rts()` to the full dataset, including the trials the original study excluded, the mixture model catches 91.5% of the trials the hard cutoffs flagged. The 14 missed trials fall just below the 0.5 threshold, with contaminant probabilities of 0.30–0.49, and are borderline cases near the cutoff boundaries. More importantly, the mixture model additionally flags 143 trials *within* the 180 ms–3 s range that the hard cutoffs miss entirely: trials with abnormally long RTs (median 2.1 s) that the mixture model identifies as distributional outliers from the shape of the RT distribution. On the slow side, then, the mixture approach recovers nearly all the exclusions the cutoffs make and adds outliers that fixed thresholds cannot reach. That advantage should not be generalized to the fast side: the simulation above shows that premature responses near the leading edge are the case the flags are worst at, and a real dataset provides no ground truth against which that could be checked.

## What This Study Does Not Cover

Two assumptions bound everything above, and both could matter in real data.

The first is that contamination is discrete: a trial is either generated by the decision process or by a contaminant process, with nothing in between. Attention also fluctuates in degree, and a participant who is partly disengaged may produce trials with a genuinely reduced drift rather than a replaced one [@adam2015lapses]. Such graded degradation is not a contaminant in the sense any method tested here recognizes, and the zero-drift process is best read as its limiting case rather than as a model of it. If disengagement in a dataset is mostly graded, the flags will see even less than they see here.

The second is that each participant's contamination rate is constant across conditions. Every process in this study injects contaminants at the same rate in the easy and the hard condition, and the mixed condition varies rates between participants but not within them. This matters because the appendix warns that contamination manufactures condition differences in bound and ndt that do not exist in the generating model — and a contamination rate that itself differs by condition, which is entirely plausible when one condition is longer, harder, or more tedious, would produce exactly that artifact through a route we did not simulate. No method here was tested against condition-dependent contamination, and none should be assumed to handle it.

# Parameter Recovery on Simulated Data {.appendix}

## When to Assess Parameter Recovery

Parameter recovery is not mandatory for every analysis, but it is informative as part of a principled Bayesian workflow — particularly when you apply a model to a new design for the first time, when trial counts per cell are unusual or unbalanced, or when individual-level estimates will feed into correlations. Beyond validating a given design, recovery simulations can inform experimental planning: by systematically varying the number of participants or trials, you can determine what your design needs to achieve acceptable recovery for the parameters you care about. For the EZ-Diffusion Model a single recovery run costs minutes, so there is little reason not to do it; for the trial-level approaches, budget the fitting times reported in @tbl-model-comparison.

The study reported here verifies that the three `bmm` DDM estimation approaches produce reliable estimates, and complements the extensive parameter recovery literature for DDMs [@ratcliff2008diffusion; @vanravenzwaaij2017ez; @lerche2016model]. The companion script is `scripts/21_appendix_parameter_recovery.R`.

## Simulation Design

We generated data from a DDM with known parameters (drift: 2.5 for easy, 1.0 for hard; bound: 1.5; ndt: 0.3; $\zeta_r$: 0.5) for 50 participants, each completing 200 trials per condition. Individual-level parameters were drawn from normal distributions around the population means (see `scripts/20_prepare_simulated_data.R` for details). We then fitted the EZ-Diffusion 3par, Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk), and full DDM to these data following the same `bmm` workflow used in the tutorials. We set two a-priori criteria for successful recovery: at the group level, the 95% credible interval for each parameter should contain its generating value (calibration); at the subject level, true and recovered values should correlate at $r > .70$, the conventional benchmark for treating a measure as a reliable individual-difference index. Of the two, the subject-level criterion is the practically more important one: absolute calibration can only be evaluated in simulations, whereas ordering individuals correctly is what applied uses of DDM parameters, as predictors, covariates, or outcomes, rely on.

## Group-Level Recovery

```{r}
#| label: fig-recovery-group
#| fig-cap: "Group-level parameter recovery. Points indicate posterior means for each estimation approach; error bars show 95% credible intervals. Dashed lines mark the true generating values. All three approaches recover drift and ndt accurately. The Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk) shows the expected underestimation of bound (see Tutorial 3)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "21_recovery_group.pdf"))
```

All three estimation approaches recovered the generating parameters within their 95% credible intervals (@fig-recovery-group). Drift and ndt estimates were highly consistent across approaches; bound showed the expected crisk underestimation (see Tutorial 3).

## Subject-Level Recovery

Beyond group-level means, we evaluated whether the models recover individual differences by correlating true participant-level parameters with their posterior estimates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-recovery-subject
#| fig-cap: "Subject-level parameter recovery. Each point represents one participant's recovered posterior mean plotted against its true generating value (x-axis); vertical bars show the 95% credible interval of the individual-level posterior. High correlations indicate that the estimation approaches preserve the rank ordering of individual differences. Columns show drift (easy and hard conditions), bound, and ndt; rows show the three estimation approaches."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "21_recovery_subject.pdf"))
```

Subject-level correlations between true and recovered parameters were high across all estimation approaches (@fig-recovery-subject), ranging from $r$ = `r recovery_r_min` to `r recovery_r_max` (median $r$ = `r recovery_r_median`). These strong correlations indicate that the hierarchical structure in `bmm` preserves individual differences while borrowing strength across participants, an essential property for studies that use DDM parameters as individual difference measures. The results are consistent with published recovery studies and confirm that all three `bmm` estimation approaches produce reliable estimates at both the group and individual level under controlled conditions.
